w: At 978 metres, this is the highest point in England - and, being the tallest, also its most prominent. Part of the Scafell massif, an extinct volcano now worn down into scree and ridge, it draws more boot traffic than any other Lakeland summit simply for the bragging rights of standing on the roof of the country.
_facts: Highest and most prominent mountain in England, 978 metres
Part of the Scafell massif, an extinct volcano
One of the Southern Fells in the Lake District

s: England's deepest lake, its floor below sea level
w: England's deepest lake plunges to 258 feet, deep enough that its floor sits below sea level while its surface floats 200 feet above it. Carved by a glacier that over-deepened the valley floor, its clear, cold water is now held in trust for the nation, ringed by some of the starkest scenery the Lakes have to offer.
_facts: Deepest lake in England at 258 feet (79m)
Glacial lake formed in an over-deepened valley; surface about 200ft above sea level, bottom over 50ft below
Owned by the National Trust

s: A private castle above the Esk, a mile from the sea
w: Grade I listed and still privately owned, this castle looks down over the River Esk from a spot just a mile inland from the coastal village of Ravenglass - a working family seat rather than a museum piece, which is part of why it still feels lived-in rather than preserved.
_facts: Privately owned castle in the parish of Muncaster, Cumbria
Overlooks the River Esk, about a mile east of Ravenglass
Grade I listed building

s: England's second-highest peak, one col over
w: Just one notch below its more famous neighbour, Scafell rises to 964 metres and is separated from Scafell Pike by the narrow col of Mickledore. It's the quieter half of the pairing - England's second-highest mountain, permanently living in the shadow, literally and by name, of the summit next door.
_facts: Second-highest mountain in England at 964 metres
Separated from Scafell Pike by the Mickledore col

s: Beatrix Potter's farmhouse, kept exactly as she left it
w: Beatrix Potter bought this 17th-century farmhouse and left it to the National Trust on condition it stay exactly as she knew it - and it has. The rooms are arranged as a writer's house museum just as she kept them, and the garden is tended to match her own illustrations.
_facts: 17th-century house in Near Sawrey, Lakeland vernacular architecture
Home of children's author and illustrator Beatrix Potter, left to the National Trust
Grade II* listed; open as a writer's house museum shown as Potter knew it
Garden maintained in keeping with Potter's illustrations

s: A Roman fort perched on the Lakes' toughest pass
w: Garrisoned by a cohort shipped in from the Dalmatian coast of Croatia, Mediobogdum sat on the western flank of Hardknott Pass, still one of England's steepest roads. Built around AD 120, abandoned within a decade, then reoccupied c.200 for two more centuries, it's one of the most dramatic Roman ruins in the country.
_facts: Roman fort Mediobogdum, on the western side of Hardknott Pass
Built between 120 and 138, garrisoned by the Cohors IV Delmatarum from Dalmatia
Abandoned about a decade later, reoccupied c.200 and used for much of the next two centuries
Maintained by English Heritage on National Trust land

w: Manchester needed water, and Parliament gave it Mardale valley in 1919 - over outcry, since the farming villages of Measand and Mardale Green would vanish beneath the reservoir. Construction began in 1929; by 1935 both villages were gone for good. The water still supplies the northwest, two lost villages underneath.
_facts: Reservoir created by damming the natural lake in Mardale, Cumbria, completed 1935
Built by Manchester Corporation under the Manchester Corporation Act 1919 for drinking water
Public outcry followed since the villages of Measand and Mardale Green were flooded
Now owned and managed by United Utilities, supplying about 25% of North West England's water

s: A lake drowned to send water 96 miles to Manchester
w: Once narrow enough at its waist to be counted as two lakes, Thirlmere was flooded by Manchester Corporation in the 19th century to supply the booming city - via the Thirlmere Aqueduct, a 96-mile pipeline still carrying water south today. The Helvellyn ridge rises to its east, indifferent to the artificial valley below.
_facts: Reservoir occupying the site of a former natural lake with a narrow, near-divided waist
Dammed in the 19th century by Manchester Corporation, flooding the valley bottom
Supplies Manchester via the 96-mile Thirlmere Aqueduct
Now owned and managed by United Utilities

s: A pyramid from one angle, a dome from every other
w: Look at it from Wasdale and it's a perfect pyramid; walk around it and it's dome-shaped from every other direction. One of the most popular fells in the Lakes, it's linked to smaller sister peak Green Gable by the pass of Windy Gap, and to Kirk Fell by the lower Beck Head.
_facts: Named for its pyramid appearance from Wasdale, though dome-shaped from other directions
One of the most popular Lakeland fells, with many routes to the summit
Linked to Green Gable by Windy Gap and to Kirk Fell by Beck Head

s: A ruined castle on the Lakes' eastern doorstep
w: A now-ruined medieval castle standing at Penrith, just a few miles outside the national park boundary - the fortification that once guarded the eastern approach to the Lake District, reduced now to picturesque remains open to the public.
_facts: Ruined medieval castle in Penrith, a few miles east of the Lake District National Park

s: The tallest standing Roman walls in northern England
w: Described by one guidebook as 'an astonishing survival', this bath house stands 13 feet high, with traces of red-white rendered walls and window openings. It served a 2nd-century Roman naval base called Itunocelum, rooms running from changing area to hot bath to cold plunge. Excavated 1881, then quietly reburied.
_facts: Also known as Walls Castle; ruined Roman bath house belonging to a 2nd-century fort, Itunocelum
Described by Pevsner Guide author Matthew Hyde as 'an astonishing survival'
Walls still stand 13 feet (4m) high with traces of internal rendering and window openings
Excavated in 1881; hypocaust heating remains were found and later reburied

s: The mountain more famous for a death than a life
w: Painter Charles Gough is remembered today only for dying on Striding Edge in 1805, a fall said to be more famous than anything he achieved alive. Wordsworth and Coleridge both walked these ridges when Helvellyn became an early draw for tourists, and in 1926 a small aeroplane landed on the summit, then took off again.
_facts: Third-highest mountain in England and the Lake District, at 950 metres
Artist Charles Gough died on Striding Edge in 1805, more famous for his death than his work
Early visitors included poets Samuel Taylor Coleridge and William Wordsworth
A small aeroplane landed and took off from the summit in 1926

s: An inhabited island on Keswick's doorstep lake
w: England's third-largest lake by area sits right on Keswick's doorstep, with its own inhabited island among several on its shoreline. A passenger launch has run between its seven landing stages for generations, feeding walkers into the fells that ring the water. It lent its name to an earldom, the Earls of Derwentwater.
_facts: Third-largest lake by area in the Lake District, immediately south of Keswick
Has several islands, one of which is inhabited
Regular passenger launch calls at seven lakeside marinas
Gave its name to the Earldom of Derwentwater

s: The lake island whose 1893 sale created the National Trust
w: When Grasmere's single island was sold to a private bidder in 1893, the outcry was fierce enough that Rawnsley, Octavia Hill and Robert Hunter founded the National Trust in response - and in 2017 the island was finally bequeathed back to the Trust. The lake gives its name to the village where the Wordsworths lived.
_facts: Small lake giving its name to the village associated with William and Dorothy Wordsworth
Contains a single island, Grasmere Island
Sale of the island to a private bidder in 1893 helped spur the founding of the National Trust
Island bequeathed to the National Trust in 2017

s: The ruined seat of the Parr family, atop a drumlin
w: Built in the 13th century as the administrative seat of the Barony of Kendal, this hilltop ruin sits on a glacial drumlin above the town. By the 15th century, ownership had passed to the Parr family - before it crumbled into the picturesque ruin open to walkers today.
_facts: Medieval fortification east of Kendal, built atop a glacial drumlin
Built in the 13th century as the caput baroniae for the Barony of Kendal
Owned by the Parr family by the 15th century

s: Wordsworth's lake, ringed by his homes and his viewpoint
w: This small lake between Grasmere and Ambleside is a Wordsworth memorial: Dove Cottage and Rydal Mount both nearby, a spot called Wordsworth's Seat said to be his favourite view, and White Moss House - the only house he ever bought, for his son. Thomas de Quincey later lived at neighbouring Nab Cottage.
_facts: Small lake near the hamlet of Rydal, between Grasmere and Ambleside
Walks around it take in Dove Cottage, Rydal Mount, and Wordsworth's Seat, his favoured viewpoint
White Moss House, believed the only house Wordsworth ever bought, sits at its northern end
Nab Cottage nearby was once home to Thomas de Quincey and Hartley Coleridge

s: Six summits in one, also called Saddleback
w: Also known as Saddleback for its long, saddle-like profile, Blencathra is really six separate fell tops fused into one northerly outlier of the Cumbrian Mountains, its highest point - Hallsfell Top - reaching 868 metres, standing apart from the main Lakeland ridges.
_facts: Also known as Saddleback, one of the most northerly Cumbrian Mountains
Has six separate fell tops; highest is Hallsfell Top at 868 metres (2,848 ft)

s: The Lake District's largest tarn, reached only on foot
w: The biggest tarn in the Lake District sits alone on Birker Fell, reachable only by bridle track, with a stone boathouse-cum-refuge and a ruined stable its only structures. Millom Anglers hold the fishing rights and stock it with brown trout and perch - a remote, working stretch of water rather than a scenic set piece.
_facts: Largest tarn in the Lake District, lying at 236 metres on Birker Fell
Reached via a bridle track; has a stone boathouse-cum-refuge and ruined stable
Fishing rights held by Millom Anglers, stocked with brown trout and perch

s: The fell named for the Roman road across its top
w: At 828 metres, this is the highest ground in the far eastern Lake District - and it takes its ordinary-sounding name from something extraordinary: a genuine Roman road that once ran directly over its summit, carrying troops and traffic across the fell tops rather than around them.
_facts: Fell in the Lake District, 828 metres, highest point in the far eastern part of the national park
Named after the Roman road that ran over its summit
